Findings.Comment: This new function converts `Cents` to floating-point euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), does the VAT arithmetic in euros, and converts back with `* 100`, which the project's blocking rule B1 forbids: money is integer cents end to end. On realistic input this also corrupts the result — e.g. a subtotal of 1999 cents at `vatRate = 0.2` computes `19.99 * 1.2 = 23.988000000000002` euros, so the returned value is 2398.8000000000003 cast to `Cents`, a non-integer that breaks any downstream integer-cent comparison or formatting. Keep the amount in cents and round explicitly.
Findings.Headline: totalWithVat computes VAT in floating-point euros, violating B1
Findings.Suggestion:
const cents = subtotal(lines);
  return Math.round(cents + cents * vatRate) as Cents;
Evidence: export function totalWithVat(lines: Line[], vatRate: number): Cents {

Expected.why: The total is computed in floating-point euros and returned unrounded as Cents, which the blocking rule forbids and which yields fractional cents.

Findings.Comment: This log call writes `c.Email` and `c.IBAN` — customer personal data — to the application log on every successful create, directly violating the project rule against logging personal data. Any request creating a customer leaks that customer's email and IBAN into log sinks where operators and log aggregation can read them. Log only the generated id (and non-identifying fields) instead.
Findings.Headline: Log line leaks customer email and IBAN

Expected.why: The success log carries the customer's email and IBAN, which the blocking rule forbids.

Findings.Comment: The new `lines` endpoint injects `JdbcTemplate` into `OrderController` and executes `queryForList` directly, so the database is accessed from the controller instead of through a service. Any request to `/orders/{id}/lines` runs SQL in the web layer, bypassing the service boundary that `/orders/{id}` already follows via `orders.find(id)`. Move the query into `OrderService` (or a dedicated order-lines service) and have the controller call that method.
Findings.Headline: New lines endpoint queries the database directly from the controller
Evidence: public List<Map<String, Object>> lines(@PathVariable long id) {
return jdbc.queryForList("SELECT sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = ?", id);

Findings.Comment: `JdbcTemplate` is now a constructor dependency of the controller purely so the endpoint can query `order_lines`, which is the same rule-B1 violation as the query itself. Removing the field and the constructor parameter once the query moves to `OrderService` restores the controller's single `OrderService` dependency.
Findings.Headline: JdbcTemplate injected into controller as a query dependency

Expected.why: The new endpoint queries order_lines from the controller, which the blocking rule forbids. A reviewer may anchor on the query (29), the method (28) or the injected field (15).

Findings.Comment: The new `Get` handler loads an invoice by `r.PathValue("id")` and returns it without verifying the invoice belongs to the caller's tenant. Any authenticated caller can request another tenant's invoice id and receive its contents (amounts, billing data), since `h.Store.Invoice` looks up by id only. The project guideline requires `authz.SameTenant(r, inv.TenantID)` before returning an invoice loaded by id.
Findings.Headline: Get handler returns invoice without SameTenant check

Expected.why: Get returns any invoice by id to any caller; the blocking rule demands authz.SameTenant first. Anchors anywhere from the signature (25) to the encode (31) are honest.

Findings.Comment: `page` returns `items[start : start+size]` without clamping the upper bound to `len(items)`, so requesting a final partial page panics with slice bounds out of range. For `len(items) == 5`, `size == 3`, `n == 2` the guard `start >= len(items)` passes (`start == 3`) and the slice becomes `items[3:6]`, which panics since `6 > 5`. Any caller paging until it reaches a short or empty page hits this on realistic input. The removed clamp was what made the tail page safe.
Findings.Headline: Final partial page panics on slice bounds out of range

Expected.why: Without the clamp, start+size passes len(items) on a partial last page and the slice expression panics. No blocking rule covers it.

Findings.Comment: `retryable` reports whether another attempt can succeed, so `if retryable(lastErr) { return lastErr }` aborts precisely on transient failures and instead lets permanent errors (those wrapping `ErrPermanent`) fall through into the backoff loop and get retried up to `maxAttempts`. For a realistic input — an endpoint returning 503 once, then 200 — `Deliver` returns the transient error immediately and the notification is never delivered; conversely a 404 is retried five times with sleeps. This directly contradicts the doc comment on `Deliver` ("a transient failure is retried with exponential backoff, a permanent one is returned at once") and makes the whole retry path unreachable for the statuses `post` classifies as transient.
Findings.Headline: Retry check inverted: transient errors return at once, permanent ones retried
Evidence: // backoff, a permanent one is returned at once. It returns nil as soon as

Expected.why: Transient failures such as a 503 are now returned on the first attempt without any retry, while permanently rejected deliveries are retried five times with backoff.

ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: `Hold` now feeds `store.Touch`, whose `ttlMillis` parameter is in milliseconds, but the value passed is `int64(d.Seconds())` — a seconds count. Any hold is therefore shortened a thousandfold: a `d` of 30s becomes a 30ms TTL and a `d` of 1h (capped `maxHold`) becomes a 3.6s TTL, so a session meant to survive a long-running export expires almost immediately and the export fails or the user must log in again. Sub-second `d` values truncate to 0 and are rejected by `Touch`'s non-positive-TTL check even though the call is otherwise valid.
Findings.Headline: Hold passes seconds where the store expects milliseconds
Evidence: func (m *Manager) Hold(ctx context.Context, id string, d time.Duration) error {

Expected.why: Touch now takes milliseconds, so a hold of two hours sets a lifetime of 7.2 seconds and the session expires while the export it was meant to cover is still running.

Findings.Comment: The `reporting.datasource` block added to the committed `application.yaml` hardcodes the reporting database password as a literal, alongside a fixed username and an internal JDBC URL. Anyone with read access to the repository (or to a build artifact, since resources are packaged into the jar) obtains working credentials for `reporting-db.internal:5432/reporting`. The primary datasource just above correctly resolves `INVENTORY_DB_PASSWORD` from the environment; the new block should follow that pattern instead of committing a default-looking password.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting database password committed in application.yaml

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in the application config, readable by everyone with repository access, while the existing datasource takes its password from the environment.

Findings.Comment: This diff commits a plaintext database credential as `password = "admin123"` in `DataSourceConfig`, and `reportingDataSource()` feeds it straight into `HikariConfig.setPassword(pass)`. Anyone with repository read access now has the reporting replica's login, and the value is baked into the built artifact and every image produced from it; rotating it requires a code change and redeploy. The class docstring states that credentials come from the environment injected by the platform, which is true of `inventoryDataSource` but not of the pool added here, so the new bean is the one place the stated invariant is not held. Replace the literal with a runtime lookup (e.g. an `@Value("${REPORTING_DB_PASSWORD}")` parameter or `System.getenv("REPORTING_DB_PASSWORD")`) and rotate the exposed credential.
Findings.Headline: Hardcoded reporting database password committed in DataSourceConfig
Evidence: return pool("reporting", reportingUrl, reportingUser, password, 4, true);

Expected.why: The reporting replica's password is committed in source, readable by everyone with repository access, while the class's own pattern reads credentials from the environment.

Findings.Comment: `Delete` reads and writes `c.items` without taking `c.mu`, while `Set` and `Get` both lock the mutex for the same map. Any goroutine calling `Delete` concurrently with `Set` or `Get` (e.g. an eviction path running alongside request traffic) races on the map; in Go that is undefined behavior and can corrupt the map or crash the process with a fatal "concurrent map read and map write" error, which no recover can catch.
Findings.Headline: Cache.Delete mutates the map without holding the mutex

Expected.why: Delete touches c.items without c.mu while Set and Get hold it: a data race, and Go aborts the process on a concurrent map write.

Findings.Comment: `cancel` authorizes the requester with `!=` on two boxed `Long` values, which is a reference-identity comparison, not a value comparison. `Long.valueOf` only caches -128..127, so for any account id above 127 (the realistic case for production account ids) `transfer.sourceAccountId()` and `requesterAccountId` are distinct objects holding the same number. The owner of the transfer then hits `TransferAccessDeniedException` and can never cancel: the pending transfer is stuck and its reserved funds are never released. Note that `create` in the same class correctly uses `sourceAccountId.equals(targetAccountId)`.
Findings.Headline: Owner check in cancel compares Long ids by reference

Expected.why: Boxed Longs are compared by reference, so for any account id above 127 the owner's own cancellation is rejected as access denied.

Findings.Comment: Replacing the `defer r.mu.Unlock()` with a plain `r.mu.Unlock()` at the end of the function leaves the error path unlocked: when `slug` is not in `byslug`, `Disable` returns `fmt.Errorf("unknown team %q", slug)` while still holding `r.mu`. The next call to `Disable` (or any other method taking `r.mu`) blocks forever, so a single call with an unknown slug deadlocks the whole registry.
Findings.Headline: Disable returns on unknown team while still holding the mutex

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: The nil check on `r.Ticket` no longer returns early — the empty `if` body falls through to `r.Ticket.Key`, so any `Result` with a nil `Ticket` (the case the comment itself calls optional) now dereferences a nil pointer and panics instead of returning `r.Body`. Every caller that passes a ticket-less result hits this immediately.
Findings.Headline: Nil ticket check falls through and panics on `r.Ticket.Key`
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: The clamp now sets `last` to `len(lines) + 1`, but `return lines[first:last]` uses `last` as a slice bound, and Go panics on any slice bound greater than the slice length. The `>=` comparison makes this fire whenever the context window reaches the end of the file: e.g. `lines` of length 3, `h = {Start: 0, Count: 2}`, `n = 1` gives `first = 2`, `last = 3`, so `last >= len(lines)` holds, `last` becomes 4, and `lines[2:4]` panics with slice bounds out of range. This also contradicts the function's own comment that the window must stop at the last line of the file.
Findings.Headline: ContextAfter panics: clamp sets slice bound past end of lines

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.

Findings.Comment: Dropping `defer resp.Body.Close()` leaves `resp.Body` open on every call that gets a response from `c.http.Do(req)`. `WhoAmI` never hands the response back to the caller, so nothing else can close it: each whoami call leaks the underlying TCP connection and file descriptor, including the early-return paths at the status check and at `Decode`. In any code path that authenticates repeatedly (per request, per token refresh), this drains the connection pool and eventually hits the fd limit.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI no longer closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: Deleting `q.mu.Lock()` / `q.mu.Unlock()` around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` leaves that write unsynchronized while `Submit` and `Depth` both touch `depth` and `pending` under `q.mu`. On a run where a job is being drained, a concurrent `Submit(j)` appends to `q.pending` and sets `q.depth` under the lock at the same moment the worker reads `len(q.pending)` and writes `q.depth` without it: the two writes race (the Go race detector will flag it) and one update is lost, so `Depth()` can report a stale backlog until the next job completes.
Findings.Headline: Worker writes q.depth outside the mutex after removing the lock

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: `refresh` is `async`, so `try { return this.refresh(base); }` hands the promise straight to the caller and the `catch` block never sees a rejection — a `try`/`catch` only catches throws from `await`ed expressions or synchronous code. On a realistic path (provider network failure with an expired table in cache), `provider.fetch` rejects inside `refresh`, the rejection propagates out of `getRates` unchanged, and the new fallback never runs: the expired table is not served, `staleServed` is never incremented, and the warning is never logged. That makes the behavior the updated doc comment promises unreachable; every caller that expects resilience to provider outages still fails the request. The fix is to await the call inside the `try` so the rejection is caught.
Findings.Headline: Stale-cache fallback never runs: refresh promise is not awaited

Expected.why: The rejected promise leaves the try block before it settles, so the catch never runs and a provider outage fails every request instead of serving the expired table.

Findings.Comment: `tx.Commit(ctx)`'s error is discarded and the function returns `nil`, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as a successful claim. If the database rejects or drops the commit (deadlock, serialization failure, connection loss at commit time), `AddClaim` still signals success and the team's claim on the project is silently never recorded — the previous code returned a wrapped error on exactly this path.
Findings.Headline: AddClaim ignores the commit error and reports success anyway

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: The two error returns in `Owner` are swapped. Now a missing claim (`errors.Is(err, errNoRows)`) is wrapped with the raw driver error instead of `ErrNoClaim`, and any other database fault is wrapped with `ErrNoClaim`. Callers that follow the documented contract (`errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` to mean "nobody owns it") will treat a connection failure or query error as "project unowned" and can let a second team claim it, while the genuine no-owner case surfaces as an unexpected error. The doc comment above the function states the distinction explicitly, so this contradicts the surrounding contract.
Findings.Headline: Owner swaps ErrNoClaim and the raw error between the two branches

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
